description: Solo participant building an AI-powered dashboard that analyzes NASA microgravity combustion data.
summary: Flame in Freefall is an interactive web research hub that makes NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to explore. It organizes curated records from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations (such as FLEX, BASS and Saffire) and historical spaceflight fires (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) into five modules: a filterable experiment explorer, plain-English research briefings, a conceptual flame-physics visualizer for Earth, Moon, Mars and microgravity, an evidence-based comparison view with oxygen ranges and source links, and a head-to-head analysis. It turns scattered findings into something students and researchers can search, compare and interpret, while openly flagging research gaps such as the lack of partial-gravity combustion data. It is an educational prototype, not for flight planning.
details:
The Mission Challenge

In microgravity, buoyancy-driven convection is greatly reduced, changing how flames develop, transfer heat, and interact with their surroundings. Unlike typical flames on Earth, microgravity flames can exhibit different shapes, burning rates, and extinction behaviours depending on factors such as fuel type, oxygen concentration, pressure, and airflow.

NASA investigations have demonstrated important combustion phenomena in space. For example, the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) studied two-stage combustion in liquid-fuel droplets, including low-temperature cool-flame reactions that can continue after the visible hot flame disappears. Other investigations, such as Saffire and BASS, examined how airflow, oxygen concentration, and material properties influence combustion and flame spread.

Although NASA has conducted decades of microgravity combustion research, its findings are distributed across technical reports, scientific publications, and investigation records. Exploring and comparing these findings can be challenging for students and researchers interested in future spacecraft fire-safety challenges.

Our Solution: Flame in Freefall

Flame in Freefall is an interactive research platform that organizes curated NASA microgravity combustion investigation records and historical fire incidents into an accessible, visually engaging environment.

The platform brings together five main modules:

  1. NASA Experiment Explorer: An interactive investigation catalog with filters for fuel type, gravity environment, oxygen concentration, and other experimental conditions. Users can explore and inspect curated NASA combustion research records.
  2. AI Research Briefing & Synthesis: Provides plain-English summaries of selected investigations, their experimental conditions, key findings, potential spacecraft relevance, and research knowledge gaps.
  3. Morphing Flame Physics Chamber: An interactive conceptual SVG visualizer that illustrates qualitative changes in flame appearance under different gravity and airflow conditions, including Earth, Moon, Mars, and microgravity environments.
  4. Evidence-Based Experiment Comparison: Presents comparisons across selected investigations, including experimental timelines, oxygen concentration ranges, fuel categories, and research findings.
  5. Head-to-Head Analysis & Historical Lessons: Allows users to compare selected NASA investigations and explore historical fire incidents involving Apollo 1, Apollo 13, and the Mir space station, highlighting lessons for spacecraft fire-safety research.

NASA Data and Research Foundation

The platform uses a curated dataset compiled from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigation records, NASA technical publications, peer-reviewed research, and historical accident reports. The dataset includes experimental parameters, fuel classifications, gravity environments, oxygen conditions, research findings, and source references where available.

Innovation and Impact

Flame in Freefall makes complex microgravity combustion research more accessible through interactive exploration, visual comparisons, and AI-assisted research summaries. It provides an educational environment for understanding how combustion behaviour changes in space and why these findings matter when studying fire safety for future human space exploration, including potential lunar and Martian habitats.

Limitations

This application is an educational demonstration and research synthesis prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not certified for operational flight planning or spacecraft fire-safety engineering. The Moon and Mars gravity settings in the visualizer are conceptual educational models, not empirical partial-gravity combustion datasets.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, Plotly, custom HTML/CSS/SVG. Source code: https://github.com/Niki824/nasa-flame-in-freefall. Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1EvBhKfCd6GDGUeVd9k7ihfXH2jsQ3Xh0/edit?usp=drive_link&ouid=115927807828639527121&rtpof=true&sd=true

Demo Video : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1kwYUQA8gre8kqeLr3GnqpN0lG1Uw5xOC/view?usp=drive_link

Use of SI: Google Gemini was used to help draft code, plain-English research summaries, and companion character images (NOVA, Commander Leo, Navigator Zog). All content was reviewed against NASA sources. No AI model runs inside the deployed app. SI-generated images are marked as AI-generated.
